question:
In triangle $ABC$: $AB = 5$ cm, $BC = 7$ cm and $AC = 8$ cm.
In triangle $PQR$: $PQ = 5$ cm, $QR = 7$ cm and $PR = 8$ cm.

Are the triangles congruent? If so, state the condition (SSS, SAS, ASA/AAS or RHS).
hint: Count which parts you know are equal: sides or angles?
solution:
All three pairs of corresponding sides are equal: $AB = PQ$, $BC = QR$, $AC = PR$.

Three sides fix a triangle completely, so the triangles are congruent by **SSS**, with $\triangle ABC \cong \triangle PQR$.

question:
In triangle $ABC$: $AB = 5$ cm, $BC = 7$ cm and $\angle ABC = 40^\circ$.
In triangle $PQR$: $PQ = 5$ cm, $QR = 7$ cm and $\angle PQR = 40^\circ$.

Are the triangles congruent? If so, state the condition.
hint: Is the $40^\circ$ angle between the two known sides?
solution:
**What changed:** the third side has been replaced by an angle.

$\angle ABC$ is at $B$, which is where sides $AB$ and $BC$ meet, so it is the **included** angle. The same is true of $\angle PQR$ between $PQ$ and $QR$.

Two sides and the included angle are equal, so the triangles are congruent by **SAS**.

question:
In triangle $ABC$: $AB = 5$ cm, $BC = 7$ cm and $\angle BCA = 40^\circ$.
In triangle $PQR$: $PQ = 5$ cm, $QR = 7$ cm and $\angle QRP = 40^\circ$.

Can you conclude that the triangles are congruent? Explain your answer.
hint: Where is the $40^\circ$ angle now? Is it between the 5 cm and 7 cm sides?
answer: No. The angle is not between the two sides (SSA), which is not a congruence condition; two different triangles fit this information.
solution:
**What changed:** only the position of the $40^\circ$ angle. It is now at $C$, between $BC$ and $AC$, so it is **not** between the two known sides $AB$ and $BC$.

This is "side, side, non-included angle" (SSA), which is not a congruence condition. Here it genuinely fails: draw $BC = 7$ cm and a $40^\circ$ angle at $C$, then swing an arc of radius 5 cm from $B$. The arc cuts the other arm of the angle **twice**, giving two different triangles (with $AC \approx 7.5$ cm or $AC \approx 3.2$ cm). Triangle $ABC$ could be one of them and triangle $PQR$ the other.

So you cannot conclude that the triangles are congruent. Compare the previous question: moving the angle from $B$ (between the sides) to $C$ (not between them) is what removes the guarantee.

question:
In triangle $ABC$: $AB = 5$ cm, $\angle BAC = 40^\circ$ and $\angle ABC = 60^\circ$.
In triangle $PQR$: $PQ = 5$ cm, $\angle QPR = 40^\circ$ and $\angle PQR = 60^\circ$.

Are the triangles congruent? If so, state the condition.
hint: Two angles and one side are known. Is the side in the corresponding position?
solution:
**What changed:** we now know two angles and the side between them instead of two sides.

$\angle A = \angle P = 40^\circ$, $\angle B = \angle Q = 60^\circ$, and the side between them $AB = PQ = 5$ cm.

Two angles and the corresponding (here, included) side are equal, so the triangles are congruent by **ASA**. (The third angles are both $80^\circ$.)

question:
Triangles $ABC$ and $DEF$ each have a right angle, as shown.

(a) Explain why triangles $ABC$ and $DEF$ are congruent.
(b) Complete the statement $\triangle ABC \cong \triangle \ldots$, with the vertices in corresponding order.
(c) Work out the length of $DE$.
diagram: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 360 290" width="360" height="290"><polygon points="55,154 55,250 183,250" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" fill="none"/><polyline points="55,240 65,240 65,250" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.5" fill="none"/><polygon points="167,50 295,50 295,146" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" fill="none"/><polyline points="285,50 285,60 295,60" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.5" fill="none"/><text x="55" y="146" fill="currentColor" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">A</text><text x="43" y="255" fill="currentColor" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">B</text><text x="195" y="255" fill="currentColor" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">C</text><text x="155" y="55" fill="currentColor" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">D</text><text x="307" y="55" fill="currentColor" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">E</text><text x="295" y="164" fill="currentColor" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">F</text><text x="49" y="207" fill="currentColor" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="end">6 cm</text><text x="127" y="194" fill="currentColor" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="start">10 cm</text><text x="301" y="103" fill="currentColor" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="start">6 cm</text><text x="223" y="114" fill="currentColor" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="end">10 cm</text></svg>
hint: Look for a right angle, a hypotenuse and one other side. For (b), match the vertex with the right angle first, then the ends of the 6 cm sides.
answer: (a) RHS: right angles at $B$ and $E$, hypotenuses $AC = DF = 10$ cm, $AB = FE = 6$ cm. (b) $\triangle ABC \cong \triangle FED$ (c) $DE = 8$ cm
solution:
(a) $\angle ABC = \angle FED = 90^\circ$ (right angle). $AC = DF = 10$ cm (hypotenuse). $AB = EF = 6$ cm (one other side). So the triangles are congruent by **RHS** (US: HL, hypotenuse-leg).

(b) The right angles correspond: $B \leftrightarrow E$. The 6 cm sides are $AB$ and $FE$, so $A \leftrightarrow F$. Then $C \leftrightarrow D$:
$$\triangle ABC \cong \triangle FED$$

(c) $DE$ corresponds to $CB$. By Pythagoras in triangle $ABC$:
$$BC = \sqrt{10^2 - 6^2} = \sqrt{64} = 8\text{ cm}$$
so $DE = 8$ cm.

question:
Triangle $ABC$ is congruent to triangle $XZY$, written $\triangle ABC \cong \triangle XZY$.

$AB = 7$ cm, $BC = 9$ cm, $AC = 6$ cm, $\angle ABC = 41^\circ$ and $\angle BAC = 88^\circ$.

Write down
(a) the length of $XZ$,
(b) the length of $XY$,
(c) the size of $\angle XZY$,
(d) the size of $\angle XYZ$.
hint: The order of the letters tells you which vertices match: $A \leftrightarrow X$, $B \leftrightarrow Z$, $C \leftrightarrow Y$.
solution:
From $\triangle ABC \cong \triangle XZY$: $A \leftrightarrow X$, $B \leftrightarrow Z$, $C \leftrightarrow Y$.

(a) $XZ$ corresponds to $AB$: $XZ = 7$ cm.

(b) $XY$ corresponds to $AC$: $XY = 6$ cm. (Not 9 cm: matching by alphabetical position would wrongly pair $XY$ with $AB$ or $BC$.)

(c) $\angle XZY$ is at $Z$, which corresponds to $B$: $\angle XZY = 41^\circ$.

(d) $\angle XYZ$ is at $Y$, corresponding to $C$:
$$\angle ACB = 180^\circ - 88^\circ - 41^\circ = 51^\circ$$
so $\angle XYZ = 51^\circ$.

Noah writes: "All three pairs of angles are equal, so the triangles are congruent (AAA)."

(a) Explain the mistake in Noah's reasoning.
(b) What extra information would be enough to prove the triangles are congruent?

hint: Could you draw a bigger triangle with exactly the same angles?
answer: (a) Equal angles only show the triangles are the same shape (similar), not the same size; AAA is not a congruence condition. (b) Any one pair of corresponding sides equal, e.g. $PQ = XY$ (then ASA).
solution:
(a) AAA is **not** a congruence condition. Equal angles fix the shape of a triangle but not its size: an enlargement of $PQR$ has exactly the same angles but longer sides. In the diagram $XYZ$ is clearly larger than $PQR$, so the triangles are **similar**, not congruent.

(b) You need at least one pair of corresponding sides to be equal, for example $PQ = XY$. Then $\angle P = \angle X$, $\angle Q = \angle Y$ and the included side $PQ = XY$ give congruence by **ASA**. (Any corresponding pair works, by ASA or AAS.)

question:
In triangle $ABC$: $AC = 8$ cm, $\angle BAC = 35^\circ$ and $\angle BCA = 70^\circ$.
In triangle $PQR$: $QR = 8$ cm, $\angle QRP = 35^\circ$ and $\angle RQP = 70^\circ$.

Grace writes:
"The triangles are congruent by ASA, so $\triangle ABC \cong \triangle PQR$. Therefore $AB = PQ$."

(a) Grace's choice of condition is correct. Explain what is wrong with the rest of her answer.
(b) Write a correct congruence statement and state which side of triangle $PQR$ is equal to $AB$.
hint: Match the vertices by their angles: which vertex of $PQR$ has the $35^\circ$ angle? Which has $70^\circ$?
answer: (a) She matched the vertices in the wrong order; $A$ corresponds to $R$, not $P$. (b) $\triangle ABC \cong \triangle RPQ$, so $AB = RP$.
solution:
(a) The condition is right: two angles and the included side are equal ($35^\circ$, $70^\circ$ and the 8 cm side between them). But Grace has matched the vertices alphabetically instead of by the equal angles.

Match by angles:
* $35^\circ$: $A \leftrightarrow R$
* $70^\circ$: $C \leftrightarrow Q$
* the remaining vertices: $B \leftrightarrow P$ (both $75^\circ$)

So $A$ corresponds to $R$, not $P$, and "$AB = PQ$" pairs the wrong sides.

(b) Writing the vertices in matching order:
$$\triangle ABC \cong \triangle RPQ$$
$AB$ corresponds to $RP$, so $AB = RP$. (Check: $AB$ is opposite the $70^\circ$ angle at $C$; $RP$ is opposite the $70^\circ$ angle at $Q$. ✓)

question:
$ABCD$ is a kite with $AB = AD$ and $CB = CD$, as shown. Ben is asked to prove that triangles $ABC$ and $ADC$ are congruent. His proof is shown below.

$AB = AD$
$CB = CD$
$\angle BAC = \angle DAC$ because the triangles are congruent.
So the triangles are congruent (SAS).

(a) Explain what is wrong with Ben's proof.
(b) Write out a correct proof.
diagram: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 360 290" width="360" height="290"><polygon points="180,30 90,120 180,270 270,120" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" fill="none"/><line x1="180" y1="30" x2="180" y2="270" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.5"/><line x1="139.2" y1="79.2" x2="130.8" y2="70.8" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.5"/><line x1="229.2" y1="70.8" x2="220.8" y2="79.2" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.5"/><line x1="138.9" y1="189.8" x2="128.6" y2="195.9" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.5"/><line x1="141.4" y1="194.1" x2="131.1" y2="200.2" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.5"/><line x1="231.4" y1="195.9" x2="221.1" y2="189.8" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.5"/><line x1="228.9" y1="200.2" x2="218.6" y2="194.1" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="180" y="22" fill="currentColor" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">A</text><text x="78" y="125" fill="currentColor" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">B</text><text x="180" y="288" fill="currentColor" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">C</text><text x="282" y="125" fill="currentColor" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">D</text></svg>
hint: Can you use the thing you are trying to prove as one of your reasons? Is there a third pair of sides you can use instead of the angle?
answer: (a) No reasons are given, and the angle step uses the conclusion as its reason (circular); his SAS angle is also not between the sides he lists. (b) $AB = AD$ (given), $CB = CD$ (given), $AC$ common, so congruent by SSS.
solution:
(a) There are three problems.
* The first two lines have no reasons (they should say "given").
* The angle step is **circular**: it uses "the triangles are congruent", which is what he is trying to prove. A reason must not depend on the conclusion.
* For SAS the angle must be between the two sides used; $\angle BAC$ is not between $AB$ and $CB$.

(b) **Proof**

$AB = AD$ (given)

$CB = CD$ (given)

$AC = AC$ (common side)

So $\triangle ABC \cong \triangle ADC$ (SSS).

(As a consequence, $\angle BAC = \angle DAC$: the diagonal $AC$ bisects the angle at $A$. This is now a valid conclusion because it **follows from** the congruence.)

question:
Triangle $X$ has sides of 6 cm and 7 cm with an angle of $50^\circ$ between them.

For each triangle below, decide whether it **must** be congruent to triangle $X$. Give a reason for each answer.

* Triangle A: sides 7 cm and 6 cm, with $50^\circ$ between them.
* Triangle B: sides 6 cm and 7 cm, with a $50^\circ$ angle opposite the 6 cm side.
* Triangle C: angles $50^\circ$, $60^\circ$ and $70^\circ$; no sides are given.
* Triangle D: the mirror image (reflection) of triangle $X$.
hint: Check each against the conditions SSS, SAS, ASA/AAS, RHS. Is the angle between the two sides? Do reflections change lengths or angles?
answer: A: yes (SAS). B: no, the angle is not included (SSA). C: no, angles alone (AAA) never prove congruence. D: yes, a reflection is a rigid motion.
solution:
**A: must be congruent.** Two sides 6 cm and 7 cm with the included angle $50^\circ$: SAS. The order in which the sides are listed does not matter.

**B: not necessarily.** The $50^\circ$ angle is opposite a side, not between the two given sides. That is SSA, which is not a congruence condition. (In fact, in $X$ the angle opposite the 6 cm side is not $50^\circ$, so B cannot be congruent to $X$.)

**C: not necessarily.** Equal angles only give the shape, not the size (AAA proves similarity at most), and no side is given. (In fact $X$'s other two angles are fixed by SAS: by the cosine rule its third side is about 5.57 cm and its angles are about $50^\circ$, $55.6^\circ$ and $74.4^\circ$, so C is not even similar to $X$.)

**D: must be congruent.** A reflection is a rigid motion: it keeps every length and angle, so the image has sides 6 cm and 7 cm with $50^\circ$ between them. Congruent shapes may be mirror images of each other.

question: In the diagram, the straight lines $AE$ and $BD$ cross at $C$. $AB$ is parallel to $DE$, and $C$ is the midpoint of $AE$.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Prove that triangle $ABC$ is congruent to triangle $EDC$.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Hence explain why $C$ is the midpoint of $BD$.

hint: Look for a pair of equal sides from the midpoint, vertically opposite angles at $C$, and alternate angles from the parallel lines.
answer: (a) $AC = EC$ (midpoint), $\angle ACB = \angle ECD$ (vertically opposite), $\angle BAC = \angle DEC$ (alternate), so congruent by ASA. (b) $BC = DC$ (corresponding sides of congruent triangles).
solution:
(a) $AC = EC$ ($C$ is the midpoint of $AE$) (B1)

$\angle ACB = \angle ECD$ (vertically opposite angles are equal) (B1, for one correct pair of angles with reason)

$\angle BAC = \angle DEC$ (alternate angles, $AB \parallel DE$)

So $\triangle ABC \cong \triangle EDC$ (ASA). (B1, for a complete proof with all reasons and the condition)

Alternative: using $\angle ABC = \angle EDC$ (alternate angles) instead of $\angle BAC = \angle DEC$ gives two angles and a non-included corresponding side, $AC = EC$, so the triangles are congruent by **AAS**. Either is accepted.

(b) Since the triangles are congruent, the corresponding sides $BC$ and $DC$ are equal, so $C$ is the midpoint of $BD$. (B1)

Note: "$BC = DC$" cannot be used in part (a) as a reason, because it is only known **after** the congruence is proved.

question:
Triangle $ABC$ has vertices $A(1, 1)$, $B(4, 1)$ and $C(1, 3)$. Triangle $DEF$ has vertices $D(-1, -3)$, $E(-4, -3)$ and $F(-1, -1)$.

(a) Use lengths to show that $\triangle ABC \cong \triangle DEF$.
(b) Describe a sequence of rigid motions (reflections, rotations, translations) that maps $A$ to $D$, $B$ to $E$ and $C$ to $F$.
(c) Explain why your sequence must include a reflection.
hint: Use the distance formula $\sqrt{(x_2 - x_1)^2 + (y_2 - y_1)^2}$ for the sloping sides. For (b), compare the shapes: is $DEF$ a mirror image of $ABC$?
answer: (a) $AB = DE = 3$, $AC = DF = 2$, $BC = EF = \sqrt{13}$, so congruent (SSS). (b) For example, reflect in the $y$-axis, then translate by $\begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ -4 \end{pmatrix}$. (c) The vertex order is reversed (anticlockwise to clockwise); only reflections reverse orientation.
solution:
(a) $AB = 4 - 1 = 3$ and $DE = -1 - (-4) = 3$.

$AC = 3 - 1 = 2$ and $DF = -1 - (-3) = 2$.
$$BC = \sqrt{(1 - 4)^2 + (3 - 1)^2} = \sqrt{13}, \qquad EF = \sqrt{(-1 - (-4))^2 + (-1 - (-3))^2} = \sqrt{13}$$

All three pairs of corresponding sides are equal, so $\triangle ABC \cong \triangle DEF$ (SSS).

(b) Reflect in the $y$-axis, $(x, y) \to (-x, y)$:
$$A(1, 1) \to (-1, 1), \quad B(4, 1) \to (-4, 1), \quad C(1, 3) \to (-1, 3)$$
Then translate by $\begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ -4 \end{pmatrix}$:
$$(-1, 1) \to (-1, -3) = D, \quad (-4, 1) \to (-4, -3) = E, \quad (-1, 3) \to (-1, -1) = F$$
(Other correct sequences exist, e.g. reflect in the $x$-axis, then rotate $180^\circ$ about $(0, -2)$.)

(c) Going $A \to B \to C$ turns **anticlockwise** (right, then up-left), but $D \to E \to F$ turns **clockwise** (left, then up-right). Rotations and translations keep this orientation; only a reflection reverses it. So any sequence of rigid motions mapping $ABC$ to $DEF$ needs an odd number of reflections.

Because rigid motions preserve every length and angle, finding such a sequence is itself a proof that the triangles are congruent (the transformational definition of congruence).

question:
A surveyor wants the width of a straight river without crossing it. She stands at $B$, directly opposite a tree $A$ on the far bank, so that $AB$ is perpendicular to the bank. She walks 40 m along the bank to a post $C$, then a further 40 m to $D$. At $D$ she turns through $90^\circ$ and walks away from the river until she reaches $E$, where the post $C$ is exactly in line with the tree. $DE$ measures 27 m.

(a) Prove that triangles $ABC$ and $EDC$ are congruent.
(b) Hence state the width of the river, $AB$.

hint: Look for a right angle in each triangle, the equal 40 m sides, and the angles at $C$ where the line $AE$ crosses the bank.
answer: (a) $\angle ABC = \angle EDC = 90^\circ$, $BC = DC = 40$ m, $\angle ACB = \angle ECD$ (vertically opposite), so congruent by ASA. (b) 27 m
solution:
(a) $\angle ABC = \angle EDC = 90^\circ$ (both lines are perpendicular to the bank)

$BC = DC = 40$ m (measured)

$\angle ACB = \angle ECD$ (vertically opposite angles, since $A$, $C$, $E$ are in a straight line and $B$, $C$, $D$ are on the bank)

So $\triangle ABC \cong \triangle EDC$ (ASA).

(b) $AB$ corresponds to $ED$, so $AB = ED = 27$ m. The river is 27 m wide.

This method only needs measurements made on one side of the river.

question:
A timber roof truss is in the shape of an isosceles triangle $ABC$. The two rafters $AB$ and $AC$ are each 4.2 m long, and the horizontal beam $BC$ is 7.2 m long. A vertical post joins the apex $A$ to the midpoint $M$ of $BC$.

(a) Prove that triangles $ABM$ and $ACM$ are congruent.
(b) Hence prove that the post $AM$ is perpendicular to the beam $BC$.
(c) Work out the length of the post $AM$, correct to the nearest centimetre.
hint: For (b), use the fact that the two angles at $M$ lie on a straight line. For (c), use Pythagoras in one of the congruent triangles.
answer: (a) $AB = AC$, $BM = CM$, $AM$ common, so congruent (SSS). (b) $\angle AMB = \angle AMC$ and they sum to $180^\circ$, so each is $90^\circ$. (c) 2.16 m
solution:
(a) $AB = AC = 4.2$ m (given, equal rafters)

$BM = CM = 3.6$ m ($M$ is the midpoint of $BC$)

$AM = AM$ (common side)

So $\triangle ABM \cong \triangle ACM$ (SSS).

(b) From the congruence, the corresponding angles $\angle AMB$ and $\angle AMC$ are equal. They are angles on the straight line $BC$, so
$$\angle AMB + \angle AMC = 180^\circ \quad\Rightarrow\quad 2\angle AMB = 180^\circ \quad\Rightarrow\quad \angle AMB = 90^\circ$$
So $AM$ is perpendicular to $BC$.

(c) In the right-angled triangle $ABM$:
$$AM = \sqrt{4.2^2 - 3.6^2} = \sqrt{17.64 - 12.96} = \sqrt{4.68} = 2.1633\ldots\text{ m}$$
$AM \approx 2.16$ m (to the nearest centimetre).

Note that part (b) is what justifies using Pythagoras in part (c): we had to **prove** the right angle, not assume it.

question:
$ABCD$ is a square. $E$ is a point on $BC$ and $F$ is a point on $CD$ such that $BE = CF$. The lines $AE$ and $BF$ meet at $G$.

(a) Prove that $AE = BF$.
(b) Prove that $AE$ is perpendicular to $BF$.
diagram: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 360 290" width="360" height="290"><polygon points="60,30 300,30 300,270 60,270" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" fill="none"/><line x1="60" y1="30" x2="300" y2="120" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="300" y1="30" x2="210" y2="270" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2"/><polyline points="290,30 290,40 300,40" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.5" fill="none"/><polyline points="300,260 290,260 290,270" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.5" fill="none"/><polyline points="70,270 70,260 60,260" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.5" fill="none"/><polyline points="60,40 70,40 70,30" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.5" fill="none"/><text x="48" y="35" fill="currentColor" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">A</text><text x="312" y="35" fill="currentColor" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">B</text><text x="312" y="282" fill="currentColor" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">C</text><text x="48" y="282" fill="currentColor" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">D</text><text x="312" y="125" fill="currentColor" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">E</text><text x="210" y="288" fill="currentColor" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">F</text><text x="258.4" y="122.9" fill="currentColor" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="end">G</text></svg>
hint: Find two congruent triangles, one containing $AE$ and one containing $BF$, each with a right angle at a corner of the square. For (b), look at the angles of triangle $ABG$.
answer: (a) $\triangle ABE \cong \triangle BCF$ (SAS), so $AE = BF$. (b) $\angle BAE = \angle CBF$, so in triangle $ABG$ the angles at $A$ and $B$ add up to $90^\circ$, giving $\angle AGB = 90^\circ$.
solution:
(a) Consider triangles $ABE$ and $BCF$.

$AB = BC$ (sides of a square)

$\angle ABE = \angle BCF = 90^\circ$ (angles of a square)

$BE = CF$ (given)

So $\triangle ABE \cong \triangle BCF$ (SAS), with $A \leftrightarrow B$, $B \leftrightarrow C$, $E \leftrightarrow F$. Hence the corresponding sides $AE$ and $BF$ are equal.

(b) From the congruence, $\angle BAE = \angle CBF$ (corresponding angles). Call this angle $x$.

At $B$: $\angle ABG + \angle CBF = \angle ABC = 90^\circ$, so $\angle ABG = 90^\circ - x$.

In triangle $ABG$, $\angle GAB = \angle BAE = x$, so
$$\angle AGB = 180^\circ - x - (90^\circ - x) = 90^\circ$$

So $AE$ is perpendicular to $BF$.

(Another view: a rotation of $90^\circ$ about the centre of the square maps $A \to B$, $B \to C$, $E \to F$, so it maps the segment $AE$ onto $BF$, turning it through $90^\circ$.)

question:
In triangle $ABC$, $AB = 8$ cm, $BC = 5$ cm and $\angle BAC = 30^\circ$.

(a) Let $AC = x$ cm. Use the cosine rule to show that $x^2 - 8\sqrt{3}\,x + 39 = 0$.
(b) Hence show that there are two different possible triangles, giving the exact values of $x$.
(c) Explain what this shows about using "two sides and a non-included angle" (SSA) to prove congruence.
(d) If instead $BC = 10$ cm (with $AB = 8$ cm and $\angle BAC = 30^\circ$ unchanged), show that only one triangle is possible.
hint: The cosine rule with the angle at $A$: $BC^2 = AB^2 + AC^2 - 2 \times AB \times AC \cos A$, and $\cos 30^\circ = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$. A length must be positive.
answer: (a) Shown (b) $x = 4\sqrt{3} + 3$ or $x = 4\sqrt{3} - 3$ (both positive) (c) The same SSA data give two non-congruent triangles, so SSA does not prove congruence. (d) $x = 4\sqrt{3} \pm 2\sqrt{21}$; only $4\sqrt{3} + 2\sqrt{21}$ is positive.
solution:
(a) Cosine rule with the angle at $A$ (opposite side $BC$):
$$5^2 = 8^2 + x^2 - 2 \times 8 \times x \cos 30^\circ$$
$$25 = 64 + x^2 - 16x \times \tfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} = 64 + x^2 - 8\sqrt{3}\,x$$
$$x^2 - 8\sqrt{3}\,x + 39 = 0$$

(b) Quadratic formula:
$$x = \frac{8\sqrt{3} \pm \sqrt{192 - 156}}{2} = \frac{8\sqrt{3} \pm 6}{2} = 4\sqrt{3} \pm 3$$
$4\sqrt{3} \approx 6.93$, so $x \approx 9.93$ or $x \approx 3.93$. Both are positive, so there are **two** different triangles.

(c) Both triangles have $AB = 8$, $BC = 5$ and $\angle A = 30^\circ$, but different third sides, so they are not congruent. Hence SSA cannot be a congruence condition (the "ambiguous case"). Here the given angle is opposite the **shorter** of the two given sides.

(d) Now $100 = 64 + x^2 - 8\sqrt{3}\,x$, so $x^2 - 8\sqrt{3}\,x - 36 = 0$:
$$x = \frac{8\sqrt{3} \pm \sqrt{192 + 144}}{2} = \frac{8\sqrt{3} \pm 4\sqrt{21}}{2} = 4\sqrt{3} \pm 2\sqrt{21}$$
$2\sqrt{21} \approx 9.17 > 4\sqrt{3} \approx 6.93$, so the minus sign gives a negative length. Only $x = 4\sqrt{3} + 2\sqrt{21} \approx 16.1$ cm is possible: one triangle. When the angle is opposite the longer given side, SSA does fix the triangle (RHS is the special case where that angle is $90^\circ$).

question:
$ABC$ is a triangle. Equilateral triangles $ABP$ and $ACQ$ are drawn on the outside of sides $AB$ and $AC$, as shown.

(a) Prove that $PC = BQ$.
(b) Describe a single rotation that maps triangle $PAC$ onto triangle $BAQ$. Hence find the acute angle between the lines $PC$ and $BQ$.
diagram: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 360 290" width="360" height="290"><polygon points="165,175 80,255 270,245" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" fill="none"/><polygon points="165,175 80,255 53.2,141.4" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" fill="none"/><polygon points="165,175 270,245 278.1,119.1" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" fill="none"/><line x1="53.2" y1="141.4" x2="270" y2="245" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.5" stroke-dasharray="5 4"/><line x1="80" y1="255" x2="278.1" y2="119.1" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.5" stroke-dasharray="5 4"/><text x="165" y="163" fill="currentColor" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">A</text><text x="70" y="269" fill="currentColor" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">B</text><text x="282" y="257" fill="currentColor" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">C</text><text x="41.2" y="139.4" fill="currentColor" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">P</text><text x="290.1" y="117.1" fill="currentColor" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">Q</text></svg>
hint: Look for two triangles that share the vertex $A$: one containing $PC$ and one containing $BQ$. Write each angle at $A$ as $60^\circ$ plus $\angle BAC$.
answer: (a) $\triangle PAC \cong \triangle BAQ$ (SAS: $PA = BA$, $AC = AQ$, $\angle PAC = \angle BAQ = 60^\circ + \angle BAC$), so $PC = BQ$. (b) Rotation $60^\circ$ about $A$ (anticlockwise in the diagram); the angle between $PC$ and $BQ$ is $60^\circ$.
solution:
(a) Consider triangles $PAC$ and $BAQ$.

$PA = BA$ (sides of equilateral triangle $ABP$)

$AC = AQ$ (sides of equilateral triangle $ACQ$)

$\angle PAC = \angle PAB + \angle BAC = 60^\circ + \angle BAC$

$\angle BAQ = \angle BAC + \angle CAQ = \angle BAC + 60^\circ$

so $\angle PAC = \angle BAQ$ (each is $60^\circ$ more than $\angle BAC$). This is the angle between the two pairs of equal sides.

So $\triangle PAC \cong \triangle BAQ$ (SAS), and the corresponding sides give $PC = BQ$.

(b) A rotation about $A$ through $60^\circ$ (anticlockwise as drawn) sends $P$ to $B$, because $AP = AB$ and $\angle PAB = 60^\circ$. The same rotation sends $C$ to $Q$, because $AC = AQ$ and $\angle CAQ = 60^\circ$ in the same turning direction. $A$ is fixed. So this rotation maps triangle $PAC$ onto triangle $BAQ$ (a rigid motion, which also confirms the congruence).

A rotation through $60^\circ$ turns every line through $60^\circ$, so the line $PC$ is mapped onto the line $BQ$ and the angle between them is $60^\circ$.
